youtube_title: Money Sent by Mistake — and the Recipients Got to Keep It (This Time) 🦝⚖️
caption: Australia's High Court (2014) let Hills and Bosch keep payments made to them by mistake because, in good faith, they had given up pursuing real debts in reliance on them. Not a license to spend a windfall.
script: A company got money that was sent by mistake, and Australia's highest court said they could keep it. [disclaimer] This is Australia's top court, in twenty fourteen. A finance company got tricked by a scam. A businessman made fake bills for equipment from two suppliers, Hills Industries and Bosch. The finance company paid those suppliers. Then it found out the bills were fake! And it wanted the money back. Normally? If someone pays you by mistake, you have to give it back. But Hills and Bosch had no idea about the scam. When the money showed up, they thought it was payment for real debts that business owed them. So they stopped chasing those debts. And they kept doing business with that group. Because of that money, they gave something up. And the court said, every single judge, you don't have to pay it back! The question was whether keeping the money would be unfair, looking at everything. And since they'd given up real debts, it wasn't unfair. Here's the limit. This only works if you acted in good faith, and you truly gave something up because of the payment. If random money hits your bank account and you run out and spend it, that's not this case. script_old: Someone sent money by mistake, and the companies that received it won the right to keep it, in this particular case. This is Australia's High Court, in twenty fourteen. A finance company, AFSL, was tricked by a fraud. A director in a business group created false invoices for equipment from two suppliers, Hills Industries and Bosch Security Systems. AFSL paid those suppliers, then discovered the invoices were fake, and wanted its money back. Normally, money paid by mistake can be recovered. But Hills and Bosch weren't in on the fraud. When the money arrived, they treated it as payment of real debts the business group owed them. They stopped chasing those debts, and they kept trading with the group. They had changed their position because of that money. The High Court unanimously said they didn't have to repay. The test was whether keeping the money would be inequitable in all the circumstances, and given what they'd given up, it wasn't. Here's the limit. This defense depends on good faith, and on genuinely changing your position because of the payment. If a surprise deposit hits your account and you rush out to spend it, that's not this case, and you can still be made to pay it back. [loop] So if money ever lands in your account by mistake, remember
